questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Dynamic weighted intervals appear in scheduling systems, database query optimization, and ad tech (frequency capping). This problem tests understanding of range update structures, order statistics, and merging techniques for hybrid data structures.

## Key Concepts
- Coordinate compression maps real-valued interval endpoints to contiguous indices
- Segment tree provides O(log N) node coverage for any interval
- Per-node hash map (weight → count) efficiently handles duplicate weights
- K-th selection uses binary search on weight values, aggregating counts across O(log N) nodes per check

## Data Layout
Each segment tree node maintains a Map<number, number> where keys are interval weights and values are counts of intervals with that weight covering the node's range. The root covers all compressed coordinates; leaves represent single points.

## Handling Duplicates
Instead of storing raw multisets, use a frequency map. When adding an interval with weight w, increment map[w]; when removing, decrement. Zero entries are deleted to keep maps small. This supports O(1) weight lookups and accurate counting.

## K-th Selection Process
1. Gather all node maps along the path from root to leaf for point x
2. Binary search on weight value in range [minWeight, maxWeight]
3. For each candidate, sum all counts where weight >= candidate across all nodes
4. Find smallest weight where cumulative count >= k (k-th largest)

Time complexity: O(log N * log W) per operation, where N is coordinate count and W is weight range.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to combine deque operations with real-time median maintenance, including duplicates and lazy deletions, under amortized log-time guarantees.

## Key Concepts
- Median maintenance with two multisets/heaps
- Lazy deletion to handle arbitrary pops from either end
- Balancing invariants to retrieve lower median for even sizes

## Code Example
```pseudo
class MedianDeque:
  left: Multiset // max-heap behavior
  right: Multiset // min-heap behavior
  delLeft, delRight: Map

  pushFront(x): insert into left; rebalance
  pushBack(x): insert into right; rebalance
  popFront(): mark in delLeft; prune; rebalance
  popBack(): mark in delRight; prune; rebalance
  median(): return max(left) if |left| > |right| else max(left)
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this for a sliding window median over a fixed-size window?
- What are the memory implications of lazy deletions and how would you bound them over time?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests mastering of dynamic trees for weighted path queries, a practical need in graph-based workloads with frequent updates.

## Key Concepts
- Link-Cut Tree (LCT) with edge-nodes representation
- Path queries via expose/access and splay aggregations
- Maintaining order statistics across edge-nodes on a path for kthLargest

## Code Example

```javascript
// Pseudo: LCT node with weight, sum, and multiset for path k-th largest
class EdgeNode { constructor(weight, id) { this.weight = weight; this.sum = weight; /* plus pointers */ } }
```
